title: An actor in a play
hook: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote; your job is to play the part well (Enchiridion 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paul, who wrote weep with them that weep. Your line was with them, steady.

The school play is cast, and a kid who wanted the lead is the third tree from the left. One version of that kid sulks through every rehearsal. Another decides to be the best third tree the school has ever seen: swaying in the wind on cue, rustling at the sad part. The parents in the audience notice that tree. Nobody chose their role, and the play didn't care. What they did with it was theirs. Epictetus took the theater and made it a picture of a life.
screen: `THE THIRD TREE FROM THE LEFT.` → `SULK, OR SWAY ON CUE.` → `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY.`

segments.voice: Remember, Epictetus says in section seventeen, that you are an actor in a play, and the play is as the author wants it. If short, then short. If long, then long. If the author wants you to play a poor man, play even that one well. Or someone lame, or an official, or a private citizen. He lists them flatly, beggar and governor side by side, as if they were just costumes. Then the line that splits the work. Your business, he says, is to play the given part well. Choosing the part belongs to another. Who is the author? The section doesn't say. Elsewhere Epictetus speaks of God or Zeus; some modern readers hear nature, or circumstance, or simply the hand you were dealt. Either way, the split is the same. Casting isn't yours. Acting is. The Greek for actor was hypokrites. English took it over and it slid into hypocrite: someone acting a part that isn't true. Epictetus means the opposite. Play your part truly, with your whole self. Centuries later Shakespeare wrote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players". Epictetus puts the weight elsewhere: merely, maybe, but the playing is everything you get to do. Parent, patient, new hire, caregiver, the one who stayed home this year. If someone hands you the third tree, sway like you mean it.
screen: `THE PLAY IS AS THE AUTHOR WANTS.` · `A POOR MAN, A RULER, PLAY IT WELL.` · `CASTING ISN'T YOURS; ACTING IS.` · `HYPOKRITES: THE ACTOR.` · then, large: `PLAY THE PART WELL.`

segments.voice: Name today's part plainly, the way a program would list it: tired parent, new employee, patient in a waiting room, friend who has to say something hard. Don't judge whether it's a good part. Picture one scene ahead of you, and see yourself playing it well: the tone of voice, the small gesture, the line delivered kindly.
Hypokrites. The Greek word for actor, which slid into English as hypocrite. Epictetus' picture of a life: the part is given, short or long, rich or poor; your work is to play it well. Today's word.
Your line: play the part well. Even the third tree can be played with your whole self. Day three hundred forty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism think of their circumstances as a role they didn't choose, and put their effort into playing it well.
